newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Long haul to solve Japan railway debt.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Long haul to solve Japan railway debt.

text.p: Japan faces a long haul in sorting out the massive debts left from its defunct national railways, with officials apparently hesitant to admit that at the end of the line, it will be taxpayers must shoulder the burden.

"We are working to come up with a plan within this year. Depending on what choices we make, I cannot deny the possibility that there may be frictions," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told a news conference on Tuesday, referring to the railway debt.

Japan's railway debt swelled to 28.1 trillion yen ($242 billion) as of April this year from 25.5 trillion yen ($219 billion) in 1987, when state-owned Japanese National Railways (JNR) was privatised and the government inherited nearly two-thirds of its debt.
The burden taxpayers must bear to dispose of the debt is estimated at around 20 trillion yen ($172 billion).
The heavily indebted JNR was privatised and split into seven Japan Railways (JR) group companies, which took the other one-third of the debt.

The government had hoped to slash the debt by selling land owned by JNR and listing state-owned shares in JR firms, but these steps have been delayed by speculative land and stock sales during the "bubble" of the late 1980s, followed by a slump in asset prices.
Meanwhile, interest payments have grown.

The government body in charge of railway firm assets has recently started selling real estate. It raised 1.05 trillion yen ($9.0 billion) in revenue from the sales in the fiscal year ended on March 31, 1997.
It sees about five trillion yen ($43.1 billion) of revenues from selling the remaining state-owned JNR shares and real estate.
A task force within the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) was due to come up with a plan in June, but a solution anytime soon is unlikely, LDP officials said.

"It's very difficult to converge all the views. We won't be able to come up with something concrete by June and it may even be difficult to have a basic plan by the end of August," said Yoshiyuki Kamei, chief of an LDP task force.
Officials at the Transport Ministry said it will come up with its own solution to the debt problem when it presents budget requests to the Finance Ministry in August.
But the Transport Ministry budget may face a drastic overhaul before being finalised in December, depending on the LDP's railway debt solution, they said.
A government plan for sweeping fiscal reforms unveiled on Tuesday listed options for solving the massive debt, but stopped short of making suggestions on which ones to pick.
The listed choices included raising taxes, asking JNR to shoulder more debt, and issuing interest-free government bonds with the promise of easing inheritance taxes.
Other options include cutting state spending, using tax revenues designated for special purposes, and switching debts to low-interest loans to alleviate interest payments.
"Personally speaking, putting the burden on JR companies is impossible. They are already heavy with debt and you have to consider what overseas investors will think," Kamei said.

Politicians would face public anger if they raise taxes too soon after an unpopular sales tax increase in April and a decision two years ago to use 685 billion yen ($5.90 billion) in tax money to clean up a mess involving mortgage firms, which overlent during the bubble economy.

Issuing government bonds would go against a government pledge to slash the state deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2003 and would distort the overall tax system, finance ministry officials said.
Hiroshi Kato, head of the government's tax panel, said Japan should separate interest payments, estimated to be around 1.5 trillion yen ($12.9 billion) annually, from the debt.
Japan should use tax revenues designated for special purposes, such as for building roads and airports, to cover the annual interest payments, he said.
But analysts said that using tax revenues designated for special purposes would be opposed taxpayers and also by the Construction Ministry.

As for the rest of the debt, Kato said it should be dealt with along with Japan's overall debt -- estimated to be about 442 trillion yen ($3.81 trillion) -- which is to be solved within the country's overall fiscal reforms.

Economists said the least friction would be caused by switching some of the borrowing to interest-free loans from the general account budget, as was done in this year's budget, but that that would not solve the problem.
